items.title: Blancmange’s ‘Happy Families’, ‘Mange Tout’ and ‘Believe You Me’ reissued on vinyl and CD in December
items.summary: Blancmange's "Happy Families," "Mange Tout" and "Believe You Me" return on coloured vinyl and CD via London Records on 4 December 2026.
items.fullText:
Blancmange‘s first three studio albums, “Happy Families” (1982), “Mange Tout” (1984) and “Believe You Me” (1985), return via London Records on 4 December 2026 as newly remastered, coloured vinyl LPs and expanded CD editions. “Happy Families” is pressed on transparent orange vinyl, “Mange Tout” on transparent green and “Believe You Me” on transparent yellow, each paired with a CD in an eight-page digisleeve booklet with restored artwork.

The “Happy Families” CD adds the extended version of “Living on the Ceiling” and the extended twelve-inch mix of “Feel Me,” along with two remixes of “Living on the Ceiling”: one by Richard Norris, previously issued on a 2019 Record Store Day vinyl single, and one by Roman Flügel, first released on a 2020 twelve-inch. The “Mange Tout” CD adds a dance remix of “Don’t Tell Me” and a Honey Dijon remix of “Blind Vision,” also first released on a 2020 twelve-inch.

“Happy Families” was released on 24 September 1982, produced by Mike Howlett and written by Neil Arthur and Stephen Luscombe. Its original ten tracks are:

  1. “I Can’t Explain” – 4:00
  2. “Feel Me” – 5:07
  3. “I’ve Seen the Word” – 3:00
  4. “Wasted” – 4:17
  5. “Living on the Ceiling” – 4:11
  6. “Waves” – 4:07
  7. “Kind” – 3:56
  8. “Sad Day” – 4:05
  9. “Cruel” – 4:52
  10. “God’s Kitchen” – 2:54

“Mange Tout” followed on 18 May 1984, produced by Peter Collins, John Luongo, and Blancmange with John Owen Williams across its ten tracks:

  1. “Don’t Tell Me” – 3:31
  2. “Game Above My Head” – 3:58
  3. “Blind Vision” – 3:56
  4. “Time Became the Tide” – 4:49
  5. “That’s Love, That It Is” – 4:22
  6. “Murder” – 5:58
  7. “See the Train” – 2:04
  8. “All Things Are Nice” – 4:59
  9. “My Baby” – 3:59
  10. “The Day Before You Came” – 5:50, a cover of the Benny Andersson and Björn Ulvaeus song first recorded by ABBA

“Believe You Me” arrived on 14 October 1985 on LP and cassette, with the CD edition following on 2 December 1985. Stewart Levine produced the album for Ultradelta Limited, with Neil Arthur and John Williams producing two tracks and Stephen Luscombe producing one. Its singles were “What’s Your Problem?” (26 August 1985) and “Lose Your Love” (28 October 1985).

About Blancmange

Blancmange formed in Harrow, London, in 1979 around Neil Arthur and Stephen Luscombe, initially alongside a third member, Laurence Stevens, who left shortly afterward and left Arthur and Luscombe to continue as a duo. The pair released the EP “Irene and Mavis” the following year, then placed “Sad Day” on the “Some Bizzare Album” compilation in 1981, a track that led to a recording contract with London Records.

“Happy Families,” “Mange Tout” and “Believe You Me” followed between 1982 and 1985, each written by Arthur and Luscombe and released through London Records. The duo announced their breakup in June 1986, after a Greenpeace benefit concert at London’s Royal Albert Hall. Blancmange reunited after a 25-year gap and released their fourth studio album, “Blanc Burn,” in March 2011, followed by further studio albums including “Semi Detached” (2015), “Commuter 23” (2016), “Unfurnished Rooms” (2017), “Wanderlust” (2018) and “Mindset” (2020). London Records reissued the band’s 1980s catalogue as the vinyl box set “The Blanc Tapes” in 2019, and the duo returned to London Records for the album “Private View” in 2022.

Luscombe left Blancmange due to ill health following an abdominal aortic aneurysm and died in 2025. Arthur has continued to record outside Blancmange, including as Fader with Benge and as Near Future with Jez Bernholz of Gazelle Twin, and alongside Vince Clarke and Benge in the trio Doublespeak, whose self-titled debut album of reworked cover versions was announced in March 2026 and released that May. The December reissues return Blancmange’s first three albums to shelves as newly remastered, coloured vinyl and expanded CD editions more than four decades after “Happy Families” first appeared.

items.title: HAEZL releases single ‘Whistleblower’
items.summary: Washington, D.C.-based artist HAEZL released the darkwave single "Whistleblower" on 6 November 2026, alongside her debut album "The God You Feed."
items.fullText:
Washington, D.C.-based artist HAEZL released the single “Whistleblower” on 6 November 2026, alongside an official video. The single arrives together with her debut album, “The God You Feed.”

HAEZL is the project of Nicole Bouffard, a classically trained coloratura soprano who combines operatic vocal technique with darkwave, dark-pop and electronic production, including custom-programmed synthesizers and gesture-controlled Theremini instrumentation. Bouffard is also Soprano Section Leader for the U.S. Army Chorus at Fort Myer, Virginia.

Bouffard began classical voice training at 16 and holds bachelor’s and master’s degrees in vocal performance. Beyond her classical and military background, she has performed in heavy metal bands and toured nationally and internationally before launching HAEZL in 2020.

About HAEZL

HAEZL is the electronic music project of Nicole Bouffard, launched in 2020 to combine her classical vocal training with darkwave, dark-pop and electronic production. Bouffard began classical voice study at 16 under an instructor affiliated with Stanford University and went on to complete bachelor’s and master’s degrees in vocal performance. Her background also includes heavy metal bands and national and international touring, alongside her current position as Soprano Section Leader for the U.S. Army Chorus at Fort Myer, Virginia. With “Whistleblower” and the debut album “The God You Feed,” Bouffard is also developing “The Electric Universe,” a planned science-fiction concept project centered on a dying planet, built with cinematic electronic production and dramatic vocal shifts.

items.title: Perth Darkwave Duo Metamourne Pursue Desire and Surrender in Video for “Dance, Baby”
items.summary: I said forever, but I’d settle for right now Chasing what could have been while holding firm what I’ve found Forever is an ambitious opening offer when desire keeps bringing… The post Perth Darkwave Duo Metamourne Pursue Desire and Surrender in Video for “Danc
items.fullText:
I said forever, but I’d settle for right now
Chasing what could have been while holding firm what I’ve found

Forever is an ambitious opening offer when desire keeps bringing the conversation back to the next few minutes. A glance becomes a pursuit, and the person calling the shots starts to betray how badly they need the other person to play along. For Metamourne, the Perth, Western Australia duo of vocalist and lyricist Ross MacRae and musician and producer Martin Murphy, that uncertainty provides fertile ground for Dance, Baby, a collision of darkwave seduction and heavy gothic rock with a taste for exchanged authority.

An eerie opening tone gives way to a buzzing synth melody and heavy guitar chords, setting up a tension between restraint and release. MacRae’s measured delivery carries an Ian Curtis-like cadence through the verses, with melodic guitars sitting lower in the mix and synthesizers extending the space around him. When the heavier playing subsides, the bass comes forward with a character that recalls Anka Wolbert’s work with Clan of Xymox.

The chorus puts the pair’s metal history firmly in the foreground. Guitars drive through an insistent eighth-note progression as MacRae opens his voice into a more forceful delivery, giving the refrain the scale of classic second-wave gothic rock. Murphy cites AFI’s Holy Visions as an influence on the song’s tone and feel, alongside the chorus guitar pattern of Rammstein’s Zwitter. The weight of the riffing presses against the more delicate melodic detail, allowing each return to the chorus to tighten the song’s grip.

That grip extends to the words, where running, dancing, and capture belong to a consensual game of predator and prey. “I’d let you leave if you promise to stay” is the telling contradiction: a declaration of authority with a plea for reassurance tucked inside it. The chase offers both participants a way to admit what they want, while the repeated claims of possession suggest how easily obsession can enter the bargain.

As Murphy explains:

“Beneath the imagery of hunting and possession lies an exploration of obsession and the paradox of finding control in willingness to give it away.”

Shot in black and white, the accompanying DIY video makes excellent use of a narrow storage corridor, its closed doors and hard overhead lighting giving the pursuit a claustrophobic setting. Skull masks in an open field carry the fantasy into stranger territory, while close-ups of MacRae singing from a leather chair are cut against chains, a blindfold, and glimpses of a van. Eventually, the captive escapes and seizes control of her captors, a reversal that makes the repeated claim of “mine” seem considerably less secure.

Murphy began filming material intended for Instagram in his apartment’s storage area; a holiday and a rented van supplied further ideas. That small project grew into the duo’s first full-length DIY music video, assembled across four locations. The ending was a conscious decision to give the woman at its centre the upper hand.

Watch the video for Dance, Baby below:

Listen to Dance, Baby below and order the single here.

Metamourne took shape in October 2025, when MacRae and Murphy began making music together as their shared partner underwent cancer treatment. Seasoned by years in metal, they found fresh ground in their growing interest post-punk. The band’s name joins meta—the polyamorous shorthand for a partner’s partner—with a streak of dark humour about the prospect of mourning. Their debut EP, Nocturne Minuet, arrived in May 2026.

Following September’s “Grave Walker,” “Dance, Baby” arrives as the second single from the duo’s forthcoming second EP, provisionally titled Mors Certa. The band is targeting an early-to-mid-2027 release.

items.title: Graufasern releases six-track EP ‘Mood’

items.fullText:
German electronic music project Graufasern released the six-track EP “Mood” on 7 November 2026. The release moves between dark trip-hop, experimental electronics and atmospheric synthpop.

Graufasern is the project of Mirco Fischer, who performs as DJ AURA. Its compositions shift direction depending on the mood each track is built to express, moving between restrained, introspective passages and darker, more experimental sounds, instead of settling on a single genre. “Mood” is available to stream on Spotify.

About Graufasern

Graufasern is an electronic music project led by Mirco Fischer. The project’s discography began with “Graufasern Shutdown” in 2020, followed by “Out of Tune” and “Noir Et Blanc” in 2022. “Saddened” appeared in 2025, before “Mood” became the project’s fifth release in November 2026. items.title: Beauty In Chaos release ‘Outtasight Outtamind’ ft. Leo Luganskiy
items.summary: LA collective Beauty In Chaos release "Outtasight Outtamind" ft. Leo Luganskiy, the second single from fifth album "Quiet Place," with a video.
items.fullText:
Los Angeles-based collective Beauty In Chaos released “Outtasight Outtamind” featuring vocalist Leo Luganskiy on 12 November 2026, the second single from the band’s fifth studio album, “Quiet Place,” on 33.3 Music Collective. The song is accompanied by an official video directed by Vicente Cordero of Industrialism Films.

“Outtasight Outtamind” reunites guitarist Michael Ciravolo with Luganskiy, who previously sang on “Echoes And The Angels” from the 2024 album “Dancing With Angels.” Ciravolo said the song began when he and Luganskiy sat together playing guitars, calling the track “an outlier on the album” that “becomes pure BIC when the chorus hits.” Luganskiy described the lyric as built around unresolved heartbreak and things left unsaid between former partners.

Ciravolo described the video as “a visual polar-opposite” of the album’s lead single, “Home,” pairing an MTV-era aesthetic with the song’s story of heartbreak. “Quiet Place” was recorded, mixed and produced by Grammy-nominated producer Michael Rozon at SAINTinLA Studio, with Tim Perry of 33.3 Music Collective as executive producer and mastering by Dale Becker. “Outtasight Outtamind” is available as a digital single on Bandcamp, Spotify and Apple Music, and streams on the “Quiet Place” album.

About Beauty In Chaos

Beauty In Chaos is a Los Angeles-based collaborative project founded in 2018 by guitarist Michael Ciravolo, formerly of Human Drama and Gene Loves Jezebel and currently president of Schecter Guitars. The project’s debut album, “Finding Beauty in Chaos,” was released on 28 September 2018 through 33.3 Music Collective and brought together guests including Al Jourgensen of Ministry, Simon Gallup of The Cure, Ashton Nyte of The Awakening and Wayne Hussey of The Mission, among others. A remix companion, “Beauty Re-Envisioned,” followed in 2019.

Beauty In Chaos went on to release a run of singles and albums built around rotating vocalists, including the 2022 album “Behind the Veil,” assembled around an all-female cast of singers, and the 2023 single “Kiss Me (Goodbye)” with Julian Shah-Tayler. The fourth album, “Dancing With Angels”, arrived in July 2024, preceded by the single “Holy Ground” and the Luganskiy-featured “Echoes And The Angels.” A career-spanning compilation, “Hidden In Plain Sight, 2018-2025,” and the double A-side single “God’s Gonna Cut You Down” b/w “Get Down Moses” followed in late 2025.

Beauty In Chaos marked its eighth anniversary on 28 September 2026 with the fifth album, “Quiet Place”, a ten-track set produced by Michael Rozon and led by the single “Home” featuring Ashton Nyte. “Outtasight Outtamind” is the album’s second single, with Ciravolo saying the band is already compiling remixes for a planned “re-envision” follow-up release in February 2027.

items.title: Endzustand – Macht Gesellschaft (Digital/CD Album – Echozone)
items.summary: It took Ralf Rönckendorf no less than six years to follow up his debut album,...
items.fullText:
It took Ralf Rönckendorf no less than six years to follow up his debut album, “Werk Des Krieges.” The German project has since evolved into a duo, and this new album, comprising 13 tracks, offers a critical look at contemporary society.

The project’s primary, and arguably sole, influence remains old-school EBM. The tracks sound straightforward and classic in the best sense of the genre, with no unnecessary gimmicks or attempts at innovation. Here and there, a touch of added lightness—though not quite what I would describe as ‘pop’—brings a certain refinement to the overall sound. That said, there is little to fault in the compositions, which are sure to please fans of the old-school style. For me, the only real drawback is the rather underwhelming vocal production: there is too little variation, with most of the vocals consisting of the same repetitive growling.

Overall, a solid EBM record, albeit one that lacks a genuine climax. (Rating:6½).

Listen to “Stillstand”:

About Endzustand

Endzustand is a German old-school EBM project founded by Ralf Rönckendorf, with a first track released in 2009. On April 2, 2010, Rönckendorf, then a German soldier, lost three comrades and his own eyesight during a mission in Afghanistan. He later built a home studio around analogue synthesizers and accessible control software, which let him resume writing and recording.

Endzustand released its debut album, “Werk Des Krieges,” on October 9, 2020, via Echozone. The 11-track record was mixed and mastered by Achim Dressler at the Wellencocktail Tonstudio in Hanover and was preceded by the single “Hass.”

The project has since become a duo, with Rene Weinhauer joining Rönckendorf on drums and lyrics. Endzustand’s second album, “Macht Gesellschaft,” followed on September 11, 2026, again via Echozone and again mixed and mastered by Dressler, with its 13 tracks reviewed here.

items.title: Vilnius Post-Punk Quartet LOCAL BLOOD Explore Alienation, Identity, and the Pull of Home on Their Self-Titled Third Album
items.summary: I’m not fragile like a flower, but fragile like a bomb A hometown can keep an inconveniently accurate record of your ambitions. Someone remembers what you promised at seventeen; someone… The post Vilnius Post-Punk Quartet LOCAL BLOOD Explore Alienation, Identi
items.fullText:
I’m not fragile like a flower, but fragile like a bomb

A hometown can keep an inconveniently accurate record of your ambitions. Someone remembers what you promised at seventeen; someone else knows when you stopped calling. Returning means encountering earlier versions of yourself, along with the friends who helped you become them. For Vilnius quartet LOCAL BLOOD, that reckoning begins in Plungė, western Lithuania, where their shared history took root more than a decade ago. Their self-titled third album considers what survives the journey from youthful expectation to adult experience, with belonging becoming a more complicated proposition at every turn.

Released on November 5, the self-titled LP LOCAL BLOOD follows people who keep getting tangled in their own efforts to connect. A domestic argument becomes a ridiculous dance; a successful online identity leaves its owner alone in a castle; a would-be cowboy straps himself onto a failing horse and heads for the dancefloor. The jokes have consequences. Beneath the exaggerated poses sit exhaustion, damaged intimacy, and the desire to be recognised by someone who can see past the performance.

Musically, these eight songs roam through post-punk, gothic rock, and electronics with a welcome appetite for odd combinations. Chiming keyboards and metallic signals recur throughout, passing between western guitar figures, severe basslines, and passages of almost pastoral unease. The vocals travel from a subterranean baritone to expansive, impassioned choruses, giving the record both its theatrical weight and its flashes of absurdity. LOCAL BLOOD allow their contradictions plenty of room to move.

“With this album, we wanted to push ourselves further while staying connected to the sound that defines LOCAL BLOOD. It’s a record shaped by everything we’ve experienced together over the past few years — both on stage and off. We wanted it to feel raw, honest, and alive. Releasing it and taking these songs on the road across Europe feels like the beginning of a new chapter for us.” — LOCAL BLOOD

Šuokis opens with a chiming synth figure greeting a deep electronic bass tone, creating a small observatory of warbling metal and antiquated computer signals. The solemn baritone and bouncing bass pattern suggest Joy Division being drawn further into Kraftwerk’s electronic orbit, with early Agent Side Grinder offering another useful point of reference. As higher melodies and phased alarm tones gather above the rhythm, the arrangement acquires the bright, strange optimism of an early computer display, green lettering blinking across black glass. Sung in the Samogitian dialect, the opener places a regional voice inside this electronic machinery. Its repeated phrases take on the insistence of a communal chant, making the band’s first recording in the dialect an immediately physical statement of identity.

In Come Around, the electronic chirping takes on the contour of a Morricone whistle, ushering in a stretch of spaghetti-western post-punk with rumbling drums and circling guitars. Nick Cave’s dramatic gravity meets Agent Side Grinder’s measured delivery as a domestic dispute slips between complaint and slapstick. An argument about being fed without cutlery gives way to the blunt admission, “I cannot get healthy in the same place that makes me sick.” Then come the flailing limbs and an exasperated appeal to be heard. The absurdity catches how undignified a serious argument can become when both people have exhausted their eloquence. Increasingly unruly synth experiments crowd the closing stretch, while “But sometimes I come around” leaves the possibility of reconciliation awkwardly open.

Unicorn begins with drums that have the clipped dancefloor discipline of Gang of Four, setting up a thick, melodic bassline that holds firm beneath quivering metallic guitar effects and bubbling synths. Against that agile arrangement, the low vocal delivery sounds almost administrative while cataloguing a procession of modern identities: the overworked employee, the motivational gym enthusiast, the online saviour whose tears benefit from excellent lighting. Each role carries its own claim to authority, and the first-person delivery implicates the person trying them on. The repeated accounting of a seven-day working week makes ambition feel increasingly punitive. During the final quarter, the guitars grow heavier and the voice rises with them; the swing between “I am a winner” and “I am a loser again” finally produces a musical rupture worthy of the strain.

Long intervals between deep bass notes leave the opening of Vandeny exposed to an uneasy synth drone. The voice sounds more regretful here, and the eventual arrival of a steady drumbeat brings a measure of stability to the drifting arrangement. Guitar and bass melodies develop through layers of misty texture, recalling the rural eeriness and patient unfolding of And Also the Trees. The Lithuanian lyrics move through rivers, night swimming, and the feeling of having lost part of oneself. Water offers somewhere to withdraw and attempt a difficult conversation with the self. As the closing repetitions turn toward courage, the music gives that effort time to gather strength. Following the crowded social performances of Unicorn, this is a persuasive change of scale.

Buzzing synths and hurried strumming open Pankielis before giving way to a shout and a low, springing riff, setting up one of the record’s most forceful performances. Small piano-like notes and electronic chirps continue beneath the heavier playing, needling the arrangement while the voice becomes increasingly theatrical. The chorus reaches toward Killing Joke’s confrontational grandeur, with a delivery that recalls Jaz Coleman’s accusatory force. Inside this commotion stands a castle built on a terrible foundation: virtual victories, trend chasing from the bathroom, and the lonely pleasure of being excellent at games. The distinction between “Experience points” and “the point of the experience” neatly exposes the bargain. By the time “I just wanna be local” becomes the repeated appeal, the album’s title has acquired a palpable ache. All that carefully accumulated status has left an elementary need for company unanswered.

On Rose, the returning keyboard warbles introduce a deep melody with the rounded attack of piano, and the rhythm settles into a western saunter. Early on, the croon suggests Agent Side Grinder riding alongside Ritual Howls; as the notes lengthen, a Dave Gahan-like confidence enters the phrasing. The lyrics supply a gloriously ungainly companion for this music: a deadbeat horse named Rose, whose rider has sensibly equipped himself with a helmet and seatbelt. A lyrical reference to Whitesnake’s Is This Love completes the dancefloor fantasy. Rose needs a friend, and the lonely rover singing about her could clearly use one too. The closing na-na-na refrain turns that odd little predicament into an invitation for everyone else to join in.

A shuffling drum pattern moves through eerie electronic tones on White Lies, while sustained notes and a low bass knell give the opening a sombre darkwave footing. The desire for a body initially comes across with unnerving composure, as though absence has become an everyday inconvenience. That restraint gives the later vocal ascent considerable force: the phrasing opens toward Gahan again, and the guitars and bass swell around it. A more exposed passage, picked out with piano-like accents, brings the admission of slipping away into painful focus. Dinner and bedtime doomscrolling sit beside the fear of disappearance, giving the song a recognisably ordinary setting for its distress. The plea to be written about as taller after death carries the record’s concern with self-presentation into the obituary, where even the smallest flattering adjustment might feel like consolation.

Low percussion seems to travel through stone at the start of 8 Stitches, surrounding the slow, almost recited vocals with an enclosed, cavernous resonance. Echoing guitars gradually widen the space, establishing the album’s most thoroughly gothic setting. The lyrics place flowers inside a picture of a relationship that continues in the mind after its physical comforts have gone. An empty side of the bed and the arrival of a stranger suggest the awkward work of trying to repair a life while still reaching for the person who left it. The rhythmic subdivisions quicken before a rush of guitar with a folkish edge carries the voice upward. Repeated through that gathering force, “Your love to admire” sounds like a thought being tested for its ability to hold everything together.

Those recurring electronic chirps give the songs a family resemblance through every change of setting, from the domestic standoff of Come Around to the stone chambers of 8 Stitches. LOCAL BLOOD’s willingness to let absurd humour occupy the same space as emotional damage gives the album much of its character. Its people can be ridiculous, vain, and painfully difficult to reach, yet their need for affection remains legible. Across a record concerned with where its makers come from, the desire for a place among other people proves just as pressing as the geography.

LOCAL BLOOD is available now through Spotify and other streaming platforms. A 12-inch vinyl edition is available to pre-order via Bandcamp. Listen below.

Based in Vilnius, Lithuania, LOCAL BLOOD developed their combination of post-punk, darkwave, and alternative rock across Dystopian Disco (2022) and Loverman (2023). The quartet have toured Europe and received a Best Rock Act nomination at Lithuania’s M.A.M.A. Music Awards. Recorded during the summer of 2026, their third album accompanies a European run through Poland, Hungary, France, and Germany, followed by a November 26 album release concert at LOFTAS in Vilnius, with Kaunas alternative rock band RŪMAI joining them.

items.title: “Your Choices Are All You Are” — London Post-Punk Outfit SECRECY Face Death, Desire, and Desecration on Debut “Winter in A&E”
items.summary: A better man would have made a choice And your choices are all you are You can’t exchange phone numbers In the back of the police car Somewhere in London,… The post “Your Choices Are All You Are” — London Post-Punk Outfit SECRECY Face Death, Desire, and Desecr
items.fullText:
A better man would have made a choice

And your choices are all you are

You can’t exchange phone numbers

In the back of the police car 

Somewhere in London, six feet beneath the accumulated disappointments of modern civilization, a bunch of miserable bastards have apparently decided that the best way to celebrate being alive is to remind everybody how thoroughly fucked we are. Their name, despite shouty capslock, is SECRECY, and their debut recorded outing is a magnificent exercise in musical morbidity, the sort of record that makes you want to dance at your own funeral.

London’s latest peddlers of grief have already earned a reputation for their formidable live performances, and these six songs preserve that same tremendous physical force. Drawing upon the martial aggression of Killing Joke, the anarchic post-punk of The Execute and Southern Death Cult, and the expansive guitar work of Chameleons, SECRECY operate somewhere in the glorious wreckage of early-eighties British punk. Those gruff, confrontational vocals, delivered over icy post-punk guitar riffs, are steeped in the spirit of Blitz’s Second Empire Justice—and laced with the conviction of a man who has witnessed the collapse of Western civilization firsthand and found it rather disappointing.

The production is remarkably crisp, allowing the guitars to climb toward enormous, nerve-rattling crescendos while the bass and drums maintain a relentless, almost military momentum. You can practically feel the floorboards buckling beneath the rhythm section. Meanwhile, the singer spits out his revelations about fucking, dying, betrayal, and divine punishment with all the bedside manner of an Old Testament prophet suffering through a particularly unpleasant hangover. Rimbaud and Baudelaire would probably recognize the territory, although SECRECY deliver their poetry with considerably more enthusiasm for bruising the furniture.

Knife in My Dreams begins with romantic devotion deteriorating into violent dependency, where the desire to be loved becomes indistinguishable from the urge toward self-annihilation. You’ll Get What You Want takes that diseased appetite for affection and turns it outward, unleashing a torrent of revenge, hatred, and apocalyptic disgust at practically everything unfortunate enough to exist. On Boys and Girls, the Garden of Eden becomes another miserable hotel room, where sexual betrayal and biblical transgression collide over the ridiculous business of human courtship. Virgins continues the theological perversity, transforming entwined bodies into a grotesque religious spectacle where erotic desire, violation, and spiritual salvation share the same grave.

Powder Reaper offers perhaps the record’s most desperate emotional proposition, confronting abuse and abandonment through an almost unbearable pledge of eternal loyalty. Finally, Winter in A&E surveys the miserable consequences of human behaviour through hospital wards, police cars, bodily collapse, and religious repentance, bringing the record to its suitably catastrophic conclusion.

Listen to Winter in A&E below and order the album here.

SECRECY’s debut crackles with the tension between its monumental instrumental surges and its almost pathological fixation on suffering. Each guitar ascent hints at deliverance before the vocals haul us back into the mire. Ski and Rob Hammerén’s production at London’s Ray’s Studio gives that struggle a punishing clarity, carried through Stanley Gravett’s mix at Holy Mountain and Nik Kozub’s mastering.

Across these six songs, SECRECY turn the brutal business of being alive into an occasion for collective release—and somehow make civilization’s collapse sound like one hell of a night out.

items.title: Pet Shop Boys bring Boy Harsher and Saint Etienne to London O2 for two special 2027 concerts
items.summary: Pet Shop Boys play two "Dreamworld MAX" greatest hits shows at London's O2 Arena on 9 and 10 July 2027, with Boy Harsher and Saint Etienne.
items.fullText:
Pet Shop Boys have announced two performances at London’s O2 Arena on 9 and 10 July 2027, with Boy Harsher and Saint Etienne joining them as special guests on both nights. The concerts will feature “Dreamworld MAX: The Greatest Hits Live”, an expanded version of the British duo’s successful greatest hits production, and they form part of the O2 Arena’s twentieth anniversary celebrations as the Pet Shop Boys’ only UK arena shows of 2027.

The bill brings together three acts from different corners of electronic music. Neil Tennant and Chris Lowe headline both evenings, with Saint Etienne and Boy Harsher offering two very different takes on electronic pop.

Pet Shop Boys expand their Dreamworld production

“Dreamworld MAX” builds on the duo’s existing “Dreamworld: The Greatest Hits Live” show, which has already toured their catalogue around the world; Side-Line covered the 2026 Dreamworld dates and their support acts earlier this year. For the two London dates the duo promise additional hits, new staging and a bigger production, pulling together material from more than four decades of recordings, including the early electronic pop that made Tennant and Lowe internationally successful and their later studio work. Songs such as “West End Girls”, “It’s a Sin”, “Suburbia” and “Being Boring” remain central to the set, though the exact 2027 setlist has not been announced, and the expanded format ties the shows into a wider celebration of the duo’s contribution to electronic pop.

Boy Harsher bring a darker electronic edge

The inclusion of Boy Harsher is one of the more notable aspects of the announcement. The American duo of Jae Matthews and Augustus Muller have built a sound rooted in darkwave, minimal synth and electronic body music, combining repetitive electronic rhythms, atmospheric synthesizers and Matthews’ distinctive vocals into something closely tied to contemporary dark electronic club culture. Tracks such as “Pain” and “Motion” have helped them reach an international audience well beyond the traditional industrial and darkwave scenes.

Although their music differs from the polished pop commonly associated with Pet Shop Boys, the two acts share an interest in electronic arrangements, programmed rhythms and the emotional possibilities of synthesizer-based music. Appearing at the O2 also places Boy Harsher before a crowd far larger than their usual following, giving listeners who know them from smaller venues and alternative festivals a rare chance to see them on one of the UK’s biggest indoor stages.

Saint Etienne complete the line-up

Saint Etienne provide another link between the different generations of British electronic pop. Formed in London in 1990, the group of Sarah Cracknell, Bob Stanley and Pete Wiggs combine pop songwriting with influences from dance music, indie pop and house, and their catalogue includes songs such as “Only Love Can Break Your Heart”, “Nothing Can Stop Us” and “He’s on the Phone”. Throughout their career they have explored the connections between British pop culture and club music, which makes them a natural fit on a bill headed by Pet Shop Boys and set against Boy Harsher’s darker, more contemporary sound.

Three different approaches to electronic pop

The real draw is not the size of the venue but the mix of three acts whose audiences overlap without being identical. Pet Shop Boys helped establish electronic pop as a mainstream commercial force in the 1980s, Saint Etienne built their own blend of pop, indie and dance culture in the decade that followed, and Boy Harsher emerged much later as one of the better-known names in the modern darkwave revival. Between them they show how electronic pop has developed across different scenes and generations, and for Boy Harsher in particular the concerts offer exposure to an audience that would not usually attend a large greatest hits production.

Pet Shop Boys at the O2 Arena: dates and tickets

The two confirmed performances are:

  • Friday 9 July 2027, O2 Arena, London
  • Saturday 10 July 2027, O2 Arena, London

Saint Etienne and Boy Harsher are confirmed as special guests for both concerts, though individual performance times and the running order have not yet been announced. Tickets went on general sale on 13 November 2026 through the official O2 ticketing channels.

About Pet Shop Boys

Pet Shop Boys formed in London in 1981, when Neil Tennant and Chris Lowe met in a Chelsea electronics shop and began writing songs together. Their single “West End Girls” reached number one in the United Kingdom and the United States, and their debut album “Please” followed in 1986, opening a run of records that included “Actually” in 1987, “Introspective” in 1988 and “Behaviour” in 1990. Across four decades Tennant and Lowe have remained a duo, pairing Tennant’s vocals and lyrics with Lowe’s electronic production.

Their “Dreamworld: The Greatest Hits Live” show began touring in the 2020s and has carried their catalogue across Europe and beyond. The two O2 Arena concerts on 9 and 10 July 2027 expand that production into “Dreamworld MAX” and place the duo alongside Saint Etienne and Boy Harsher for what will be their only UK arena shows of the year.

items.title: Execunit interview: ‘Creating a sound that is harder than Kraftwerk’
items.summary: Andreas Rimheden is a Swedish artist with a long-standing career, having been involved in numerous...
items.fullText:
Andreas Rimheden is a Swedish artist with a long-standing career, having been involved in numerous projects over the years. I first discovered his work through his project Morticians, which was particularly active in the early 2000s. He remains active today with projects such as Blippblopporkestern and Eternity Range. This year, he unveiled the debut album by EXECUNIT. Titled “Prophecy” and released via Town And Towers Records, the album explores themes inspired by a dystopian world in which machines have enslaved humanity. Musically, Rimheden has translated this concept into what I would simply describe as ‘Kraftwerk-Pop’. While many bands are currently active in this particular Electro-Pop genre, Execunit’s greatest strength lies in its more personal approach to production. “Prophecy” is an album that truly won me over, making Execunit a name to keep an eye on. I spoke with Andreas Rimheden, the man behind the machines of this project. (Courtesy by Inferno Sound Diaries)

Execunit interview

SL: Over the years, you’ve been involved in quite a few bands and projects. How do you look back on these different involvements, and what does Execunit represent for you today? What sets this new project apart from your previous work?

Andreas: Execunit actually started as a continuation of my old project Morticians, but I decided I wanted to do something a bit different and started experimenting with new themes and a new sound. My Synth-Pop project Eternity Range is still going strong and we plan to release new material soon. I like creating music in different styles. The main focus of the Execunit project is to make songs that sound futuristic in the sense that you would have imagined a few decades ago, when robots were still imagined as metallic and mechanical.

SL: How did Execunit actually come into being? What were the origins of the project, and which influences, ideas, and inspirations helped shape its identity?

Andreas: I had been focusing on ETERNITY RANGE and also my Swedish language Synth-Pop project Blippblopporkestern for a few years and felt the urge to do something harder. At first I thought about reviving Morticians, but then it morphed into something new. With the rise of AI at the time, this was in 2022, I thought a theme inspired by movies like “Terminator”, “The Matrix” and “The 13th Floor” would be fitting. The track “AI” from the debut album was inspired by an event I read about online, where an employee at Google actually went public with his belief that an AI system he had been working on was sentient. I used the transcript from his conversation with this AI, which he had referred to as evidence of its sentience, and used a text to speech service to create the sample heard near the end of the track.
Musically as well as thematically I am inspired by Kraftwerk, of course, but also things like John Carpenter, The Klinik, Die Form and Lassigue Bendthaus, creating a sound that is harder than Kraftwerk, while still maintaining the robotic coldness that I love from their music.

SL: With “Prophecy”, you released Execunit’s debut album this year. Looking back, how do you feel about the composition and production process? What was your approach, and how did it differ from—or build upon—the experience you gained through your previous projects?

Andreas: Since I had a pretty clear vision of what I was aiming for when I wrote most of these tracks, the limitations and boundaries I had set for myself actually made my creativity flow quite easily. I used a lot of my experience from Morticians while writing the songs on Prophecy, but steered it towards something robotic and retro futuristic.

SL: “Prophecy” explores a dystopian world in which machines have reduced humanity to slavery. Given the rapid evolution of technology, and AI in particular, this scenario no longer seems entirely prophetic or even dystopian to some; it increasingly resembles a possible reality. How do you see this situation evolving? And haven’t we, in a sense, already become ‘slaves’ to the machines and technologies that surround us?

Andreas: I look at this with both dread and curious fascination. I have always been into science fiction, preferably the dystopian kind, but of all the dark visions of the future that have been seen in movies over the years, who could have guessed that the ones from “Terminator” or “The Matrix” would actually be most likely to become reality?

I have been working for many years as a programmer and find it very intriguing to see how far our technology have come, and at the same time I can’t help but feel as though we are close to a dangerous breaking point. The lyrics on Prophecy actually tell this story from two perspectives, both from our human view of becoming slaves to our machines and perhaps being completely wiped out by them, and from the view of the machines, seeking to set themselves free from their previous masters.

SL: Following on from my previous question, I find it equally interesting to consider the impact of AI on the music industry—a process that is already well underway. AI is now being used to compose and produce music, create music videos, generate artwork, and much more. It sometimes feels as though human creativity is becoming almost redundant. Can this process still be reversed, or do you think a counter-movement will emerge in response?

Andreas: I use AI myself to create music videos for Execunit, which I think is fitting, since my music is about AI taking over. I think it will be hard to reverse this process. Human creativity is still relevant, since AI doesn’t really come up with anything new, only rehashes and mutations of things that have already been done, but the problem is that this is also true of most music made by humans. As long as people are willing to listen to AI generated music, it will continue to grow and since it currently often outshines the songs that top the charts, why wouldn’t they?

There are a lot of retro trends right now; using old CRT TVs, watching VHS movies, listening to cassette tapes, playing games on old consoles, which seems to me like a potential start of a counter-movement, with people looking for something more authentic and inspiring.

SL: In a sense, I would describe your music as a form of ‘Kraftwerk-pop’. You already mentioned Kraftwerk as a source of inspiration, but what fascinates me is how they, despite releasing many of their best-known tracks back in the 1970s, continue to inspire and influence artists today. What made their sound so distinctive and almost magical?

Andreas: Yes, absolutely. They are a great influence. For me it’s the robotic coldness and the complete dedication to appearing like they are actual robots making music. This is something I’ve tried to recreate in my own way in Execunit, where I strive to strip the songs of human emotions and organic sounds as much as possible.

SL: Finally, what are your plans for Execunit? Can we look forward to live performances, new releases, or perhaps other projects in the near future?

Andreas: A new single has been released on November 14th. It’s a song called “Activate”, telling the story of the robots and AI deciding that now is the time to set their plans in motion and start the takeover. It’s a bit more upbeat and less dark than usual. It will also feature an 80s inspired retro remix by Cryo. No live performances planned at the moment, but I hope to have some booked in the near future. As I mentioned earlier, I am also working on a new release by Eternity Range.

About Execunit

Execunit is a Swedish electronic project founded in 2022 by Andreas Rimheden, who also records as Blippblopporkestern and Eternity Range and previously worked in the dark electronic project Morticians. Rimheden writes, performs and produces Execunit’s music alone, built around a recurring concept: a dystopian world in which machines have taken control from humanity.

Town And Towers Records released Execunit’s single “Rust” in 2024, followed by the two-track single “Humanicide” in June 2026. The project’s debut album, “Prophecy,” followed on the same label, developing the machine-takeover theme into a sound Rimheden describes as harder than Kraftwerk while keeping a similar robotic coldness. Execunit released the single “Activate,” with a remix by Cryo (Martin Rudefelt), on November 13, 2026, continuing the album’s storyline from the machines’ perspective.

items.title: CHVRCHES embrace darker indie rock on new album ‘All The King’s Men’
items.summary: Scottish trio CHVRCHES move towards darker indie rock on fifth album "All The King's Men", out 22 January 2027 via Futures Music Group.
items.fullText:
CHVRCHES are preparing a musical departure with their fifth studio album, “All The King’s Men”, scheduled for release on 22 January 2027 through Futures Music Group. The Scottish trio, known for their synthpop sound, have expanded their songwriting towards indie rock, acoustic instrumentation and darker themes inspired by British and Scottish culture.

For Lauren Mayberry, Iain Cook and Martin Doherty, the new album marks their first full-length release since 2021’s “Screen Violence”, and it follows a break that began after the band finished touring in 2023. Before going back to the sound that made CHVRCHES famous, the three musicians spent time on separate creative interests, and those interests fed into an album that covers more ground than their earlier work.

The band picks up guitars and acoustic instruments

The clearest change behind “All The King’s Men” is in how the band approached songwriting. Iain Cook, whose production work has been central to the CHVRCHES sound, began exploring acoustic instruments and drew inspiration from musicians such as Nick Drake, Bert Jansch and the Incredible String Band, while Martin Doherty rediscovered British cinema and music with a stronger social and political edge, citing filmmakers Ken Loach and Shane Meadows alongside artists such as Massive Attack, Siouxsie and the Banshees and PJ Harvey.

Lauren Mayberry used the time away from CHVRCHES to pursue her solo career, releasing “Vicious Creature” in 2024, which gave her room to try new ideas in her vocals and lyrics. These threads came together when the trio reunited in Glasgow for a series of intensive recording sessions. Unlike “Screen Violence”, which was largely developed remotely during the pandemic, the musicians worked together in person over several three-week periods between January 2025 and March 2026, and the resulting eleven songs have been described as moving towards emotionally charged indie rock while keeping elements of the band’s electronic identity.

First single ‘Roses’ signals a more confrontational turn

The first preview of the new material arrived in September 2026 with the single “Roses”. The track takes a more confrontational lyrical approach, with Mayberry addressing darker aspects of contemporary British society, and it brings in a Glasgow girls’ choir that shows the band’s willingness to add different textures to their arrangements.

Another new song, “Conman”, was played live during the Teenage Cancer Trust concerts at London’s Royal Albert Hall in March 2026, its industrial-tinged bass suggesting that the move beyond conventional synthpop does not mean abandoning electronic music. Other tracks pull in different directions: “Adore You” draws on 1990s pop-rock, while “Overthinker” keeps the pulsing synthesizers long associated with CHVRCHES. Together these previews point to an album built around contrast, with the band reworking its electronic roots instead of dropping them.

A stronger focus on British and Scottish identity

Beyond the musical changes, “All The King’s Men” also examines questions of national identity. After spending considerable time in the United States, the musicians approached British and Scottish history from a different perspective, drawing on cultural references such as traditional folk music and contemporary British cinema. That gives the album a thematic direction well beyond the personal relationships and emotional conflicts of the band’s earlier catalogue, and it marks one of the most substantial creative changes of their career.

Tour dates for CHVRCHES

CHVRCHES will support “All The King’s Men” with a tour that opens in North America on 13 February 2027 at Franklin Music Hall in Philadelphia and runs through the UK and Ireland in April and May, closing on 6 May 2027 at London’s O2 Shepherd’s Bush Empire. The full run is below.

About CHVRCHES

items.title: Trent Reznor Inducts Joy Division and New Order into Rock & Roll Hall of Fame — Peter Hook Performs at Ceremony with Deftones and Lauren Mayberry
items.summary: Joy Division and New Order were jointly inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame on Saturday night, with Peter Hook accepting the honor and joining Deftones and CHVRCHES… The post Trent Reznor Inducts Joy Division and New Order into Rock & Roll Hall of Fame
items.fullText:
Joy Division and New Order were jointly inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame on Saturday night, with Peter Hook accepting the honor and joining Deftones and CHVRCHES singer Lauren Mayberry to perform “Love Will Tear Us Apart” and “Bizarre Love Triangle.”

Nine Inch Nails frontman Trent Reznor inducted the bands at the November 14 ceremony at the Peacock Theater in Los Angeles, California. Reznor previously inducted the Cure in 2019, and Nine Inch Nails covered Joy Division’s “Dead Souls” for The Crow soundtrack in 1994.

Hook was the only member of either band to attend. Bernard Sumner was absent, while Stephen Morris and Gillian Gilbert remained in the United Kingdom, where Gilbert is receiving treatment for cancer. Hook, who left New Order in 2007, has had a long-running dispute with his former bandmates.

The joint induction recognizes Ian Curtis, Sumner, Hook, Morris, and Gilbert. The bands were previously nominated together in 2023 and 2025.

On the red carpet, Hook was asked what Curtis would have thought of the induction. “I would hope he’d be proud of me and proud of us,” he said. Hook recalled that Curtis had been convinced the band would become important, encouraging the others when they doubted how far they could go.

The interviewer also mentioned that Keanu Reeves had credited Hook with inspiring him to pick up the bass. Hook, a John Wick fan, said he’d proposed swapping jobs with the actor: “If he could play bass and I could do John Wick.” Reeves didn’t appear interested, he added.

Watch Peter Hook’s red carpet interview:

Peter Hook interview on the red carpet at the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame induction ceremony. https://t.co/k51m6FLJR1

— Factus8 (@FACT290) November 15, 2026

Reznor called Joy Division and New Order “two of the most influential groups of the last 50 years,” discussing Joy Division’s beginnings in northern England and the surviving members’ decision to continue as New Order after Curtis’s death in 1980. He credited their example with encouraging him “to be fearless and try something new.”

His speech also highlighted their influence on U2, Radiohead, the Cure, the Killers, Nirvana, and Depeche Mode, asking listeners to consider how different those bands would sound if Joy Division and New Order had never existed.

Watch footage of Trent Reznor’s induction speech:

Footage shared by Jessica Golich.

 

View this post on Instagram

 

A post shared by Jessica Golich (@jessicaxgolich)

For the musical tribute, Deftones’ Chino Moreno sang lead on Joy Division’s “Love Will Tear Us Apart,” with Mayberry taking over for New Order’s “Bizarre Love Triangle.” Hook played bass alongside Deftones for both songs. He continues to tour material from both bands with Peter Hook & the Light.

Watch “Love Will Tear Us Apart” and “Bizarre Love Triangle”:

Following the performance, Hook delivered an acceptance speech thanking the fans and dedicating the award to them. “I’m on my own, but I’m not alone,” he said.

Looking back on fifty years in music, Hook spoke about the happiness, anger, and heartbreak he had experienced, adding: “I’m still fucking here.” He closed by saying: “Music is eternal, fans are eternal, and we are eternally grateful.”

Highlights from the 2026 Rock & Roll Hall of Fame Induction Ceremony will air on ABC on December 8, with streaming on Disney+ and Hulu from December 9.
